newsitem.title: USA: FX analysts see hint of Rubin concern about dlr.
newsitem.headline: FX analysts see hint of Rubin concern about dlr.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin did not signal a departure from U.S. dollar policy on Thursday but some analysts detected hints of a subtle shift in Washington's concern about the dollar's rise against the yen.

While Rubin stressed there was "absolutely" no change to Washington's policy that the strong dollar is in the United States' interest, some market participants are debating whether "absolutely unchanged" actually means a tiny bit changed.
In a speech to bank executives, Mitsuzuka said that recent yen moves were "obviously excessive" and cautioned that excessive moves would be dealt with "decisively" and in a "timely manner."
Eisuke Sakakibara, the influential director-general of the Japanese Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau also called the moves "too rapid" on Thursday.

Following earlier comments by Japanese Finance officials, the Treasury chief raised eyebrows in the currency market by saying he shared Japan's concerns about the recent weakening of the yen because of the impact on Japan's trade surplus.
"What was different today is that the U.S. shares concerns about recent moves in the yen. There is no way around it," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
In Tokyo on Thursday, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka issued one of the strongest warnings yet about the dollar's recent sharp rise against the yen.

"If Japan is worried about the impact of a weak yen on its domestic economy, on its trade balance and its relations with the U.S., then it begs the question that the U.S. probably shares the concern and perhaps shares the belief that intervention is warranted," Gilmore said.

Rubin, who delivered prepared comments on the dollar in conjunction with a live television interview on CNBC on Thursday, is extraordinarily careful in terms of how he delivers messages, analysts said. He seemed to have his ducks all in a row to deliver a message today, Gilmore said.

It would not be the first time Rubin slightly altered his mantra about the strong dollar this year. Rubin signalled in early February that he was not particularly eager to see the dollar continue its unchecked advance when he began saying publicly that the U.S. currency has been strong for some time.

But concern by the U.S. over the weak yen does not necessarily translate as concern about the dollar's current level near 126 yen. Instead analysts said Rubin may be continuing to cautiously try to deprive the dollar of upward momentum.
The Treasury Secretary might have been signalling another very subtle transition on Thursday, before the dollar reached 130.00 yen, they said.
"Any shift in policy is going to be a different shade of grey sort of thing," said Alan Ruskin, research director at I.D.E.A. Inc.

"I have no doubt that they'd like to slow this thing down ... I think they've been forced to think on their feet and been forced to change the potential threshold as far as the dollar is concerned to where they suggest the Japanese intervene. I would still guess levels above 130 are going to be uncomfortable for all parties," Ruskin said.
Rubin just returned from a six-day trip to Asia during which he denied suggestions that he discussed curbing the dollar's advance with Japanese authorities.

But on his way to Tokyo, where he discussed Japanese plans to deregulate their economy, he also expressed concerns about Japan's rising trade surpluses. However, he later said he did not believe in using currencies as instruments of trade policy.

"He was very discreet," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at Bank of Montreal in Chicago, of Rubin's comments on Thursday. "He wouldn't be pushed into saying anything other than the strong dollar is in the best interests of the U.S.

"The feeling seems to be he is willing to give Japan some time, but two or three months down the line if the (Japanese) economy is not performing, we may be beginning to put a little more pressure on.
"Obviously, if the yen continues to weaken and the surpluses start to rise we may be a little less vocal in terms of a strong dollar," Johnson said.
